items.title: Two Years of MCP Builders
items.excerpt: This week, our little open-source project, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), turns two years old. And what better way to mark this occasion than by celebrating the people who helped us build it and everyone building with it. When MCP first launched, we could not have imagined how creative and ambitious the community would get with it, or how many people would jump in to help make it become what it is today. Developers have been showing up since the very first day the project landed on GitHub, and we’ve had more than 2,500 unique contributors since then. As we’re heading into our third year, it’s worth looking back at some of the highlights since that fateful November of 2024. MCP milestones and spec releases from November 2024 to November 2026 Open from the start#MCP began in the summer of 2024, when David Soria Parra pitched Justin Spahr-Summers on an open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Justin was on board right away, and the two of them spent the next few months building it. On November 25, Anthropic open-sourced the Model Context Protocol. It didn’t take long for the community to start helping us extend and evolve MCP into a far better protocol than we ever could have built on our own. So in July 2025, we formalized our governance to make it straightforward for anyone to propose changes and have a say in where the project goes next. By the time we celebrated the first birthday, we had full support for remote servers, industry-standard authorization capabilities, and a registry reference implementation that other companies were adopting for both internal and external projects. Just a couple of weeks later, we got to celebrate again when MCP joined the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. That gave maintainers and the community the independence to keep steering the protocol together for years to come, with the same vendor-neutral stewardship as projects like Kubernetes, PyTorch, and Node.js. items.title: More predictable notifications on GitHub.com
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Starting December 1, 2026, we’re migrating notifications on GitHub.com over the course of a week to make subscriptions more predictable, correct unexpected behavior, and support the growing scale of activity. During the rollout, notifications may behave differently for different users. No action is required, but the changes below may affect how you manage and filter notifications. This does not apply to GitHub Enterprise Server. What is changing Routine activity won’t resubscribe you: Previously, after manually unsubscribing, notification activities such as commenting, submitting a pull request review, changing a thread’s state, or merge queue activity resulted in a re-subscription. Now, those actions leave you unsubscribed. Being mentioned, assigned, or receiving a pull request review request will continue to resubscribe you since those actions ask for your attention. Team-mention notifications will reflect current team membership and mentions: Previously, you could continue receiving notifications after a team mention was removed or you left the team. If you joined a team after it was mentioned, you wouldn’t receive notifications for future activity. Now, removing the mention or leaving the team stops future notifications based on that team mention, so you may receive fewer notifications. Joining the team enables notifications for future activity on threads where it was already mentioned. Other reasons, such as commenting, may still result in notifications. Removing a mention won’t stop notifications you receive for other reasons: Previously, removing a mention could stop notifications even if you’d also participated in another way. Now, if someone removes a mention, you’ll stay subscribed as long as another reason, such as commenting or being assigned, still applies. items.title: [AINews] Jensen Is Back! and OpenAI Shows Its Pretraining Curve, joined by Microsoft
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation, and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4, their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back. Eleven days after announcing his resignation, Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗ The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out, with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence, Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset… which has notable caveats): View post on X ↗ Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly. Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70. This is all in context of pacing the frontier. items.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here. It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3, Observable Plot, and topojson-client), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account. Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
items.excerpt: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. items.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
items.excerpt: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook. Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history, ai, generative-ai, llms, a

items.title: datasette-charts 0.2a0
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0 I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday. Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent, so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools. Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself: Download the video (MP4) I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me. Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video. Tags: datasette-agent, datasette, visualization

items.title: Lessons from building agents on the Claude Platform
items.author: Claude
items.excerpt: Anthropic built the infrastructure behind Claude Managed Agents three times before turning it into a platform for customers. Jess Yan (Product Manager, Claude Managed Agents), Michael Cohen (Member of Technical Staff, Claude Managed Agents), and Lance Martin (Member of Technical Staff, Claude Platform) share what they learned during the process and offer best practices for teams building with Managed Agents. They explain how Managed Agents separates the harness from its execution environment, when to use dynamic workflows to coordinate work across many agents, and how dreaming consolidates what agents store in memory between sessions.* Chapters 0:00 - Intro 0:20 - Why we built Claude Managed Agents 1:50 - Keeping up with models and managing cost 4:50 - Using dynamic workflows and multi-agent harnesses 8:10 - Scaling Claude Managed Agents: decoupling the brain and hands 10:30 - How customers are building with Claude Managed Agents 12:15 - How dreaming and agent memory work Learn more about the Claude Platform: https://claude.com/platform/api Follow ClaudeDevs on X for product updates and best practices from the Claude Platform team: https://x.com/ClaudeDevs *Claude Managed Agents and dynamic workflows are in beta; dreaming is a research preview.
